issues.subcategory: post-randomization participant exclusion based on confidence/cell counts
issues.description: Across experiments, large numbers of participants were excluded after data collection because they had too few high-confidence trials in one or more design cells. This exclusion criterion is outcome-contingent because it depends on participants' confidence behavior and cellwise response patterns, which are closely tied to the phenomenon under study. It can distort estimates, compromise representativeness, and bias Bayes factors and percentages upward by selecting participants who already produce many high-confidence responses. The problem is especially severe in Experiment 2, where nearly one-third of the sample was excluded.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion due to zero-cell counts
issues.description: The analysis excludes participants because of missing cells created by zero high-confidence responses, then uses ANOVA on the reduced sample. This is a non-ignorable missing-data mechanism: zero counts are substantively meaningful, not random missingness. Listwise deletion in this context can bias effect estimates and undermines the interpretation of the resulting inferential statistics.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: sequential stopping without full design specification
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential Bayes-factor stopping, but the manuscript does not provide enough information to evaluate error control or robustness: no prior specification for the sequentially monitored test, no maximum sample size, no exact decision protocol if the threshold was crossed and later receded, and no clarification of how this stopping plan related to the later ANOVA-based analyses. The stopping rule targeted a 'critical t-test', but the reported primary analyses are repeated-measures ANOVAs, creating substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: no preregistration or analysis plan reported
issues.description: The manuscript presents multiple experiments, model-selection steps, follow-up ANOVAs, exclusions, and sequential stopping, yet provides no preregistration or timestamped analysis plan. Given the many analytic choices—confidence thresholding, participant exclusions, collapsing across conditions after a null effect, selecting the 'best fitting' Bayesian model, and running follow-up tests—the absence of preregistration raises concern about undisclosed flexibility.
issues.quote: Because of this, in subsequent analyses all data are collapsed over the two cue types (red and blue).

issues.subcategory: contradictory interpretation of Table 4 in Experiment 2
issues.description: The text states that for non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was relevant and that error rates increased from short to long delay, but Table 4 reports BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay, which is evidence against including Memory Delay, and very strong evidence for Target Type instead (BFincl = 39110.895). The narrative interpretation is incompatible with the tabled statistics.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.subcategory: text-table mismatch for Experiment 2 follow-up ANOVA
issues.description: The text reports one pattern of Bayes factors for Table 4, while the table shows the opposite pattern. This directly undermines confidence in the accuracy of the reported analyses and raises the possibility of copy/paste or table-labeling errors that affect substantive conclusions.
issues.quote: Table 4... Memory Delay ... BFincl 0.064 ... Target Type ... BFincl 39110.895 ..." contrasted with "Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)"

issues.subcategory: inconsistent confidence scale description
issues.description: Experiment 1 reports different confidence scales in different sections. The figure caption says confidence is rated 1-4, but the Procedure says participants clicked one of two boxes from 1-2. This inconsistency matters because the key analyses rely on selecting 'high confidence' trials; the operational definition is unclear.
issues.quote: Figure 1... Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty)." and later "After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.subcategory: participant exclusion count inconsistency in Experiment 1
issues.description: The participant accounting in Experiment 1 does not add up. Forty participants remained after training exclusions, yet the analysis states inclusion of 23 participants and then parenthetically says 5 participants were excluded. This leaves 12 participants unaccounted for and makes the effective sample unclear.
issues.quote: The remaining 40 participants..." and later "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: figure numbering inconsistency
issues.description: Experiment 4 Results refers to 'Figure 5' for Experiment 4 error rates, but the next figure is labeled Figure 6. Such numbering inconsistencies suggest insufficient manuscript checking and can impede interpretation.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials..." followed by "Figure 6 Experiment 4. Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response.

issues.subcategory: incorrect reference to prior experiments
issues.description: The Discussion of Experiment 3 says the same pattern was observed in 'Experiment 1-3', although Experiment 3 is the experiment being discussed and the intended comparison seems to be Experiments 1-2. This contributes to confusion about the evidence chain.
issues.quote: participants still show the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim about all stages of STM
issues.description: The General Discussion states that 'all stages of STM are susceptible' while the manuscript explicitly acknowledges that iconic memory was not tested. This overstates the evidence and contradicts the paper's own limitation.
issues.quote: The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research" and earlier "Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM"

issues.subcategory: high confidence treated as evidence of illusion rather than bias/metacognition
issues.description: The manuscript assumes that high-confidence errors necessarily reflect 'illusory memories' rather than guessing or response bias. However, confidence is an imperfect marker of memory phenomenology and can itself be biased by familiarity, fluency, and expectations. Without calibration analyses, receiver operating characteristics, or phenomenological measures, equating high confidence with an actual false memory trace overstates construct validity.
issues.quote: Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: response format confounds memory with forced-choice discrimination
issues.description: The primary measure is selection from a six-option response display that often includes both the target and its mirrored counterpart. Errors in this format can arise from decision-level confusion, lure familiarity, and comparative discrimination processes, not necessarily altered memory representations. The task therefore does not cleanly operationalize 'memory illusions'.
issues.quote: The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.subcategory: increase over time does not rule out perceptual encoding confounds
issues.description: The core causal argument is that if illusion rates increase with delay, the effect must be memory-based rather than perceptual. But increased delay can amplify decision noise, criterion shifts, interference from the probe or intervening display, and differential forgetting of orientation information without implying that a false memory representation was 'reshaped' post-perceptually. The design does not directly isolate perceptual encoding from retention or retrieval processes.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding.

issues.subcategory: claims of reshaping memory traces are too strong for behavioral data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly claims that expectations 'reshape perceptual representations' and that correctly encoded percepts are 'being converted' to illusory memories. The experiments only observe response distributions at test; they do not track representational change and cannot distinguish altered storage from retrieval bias or decision criterion shifts. The language overreaches the evidence.
issues.quote: These experiments show that expectations can reshape perceptual representations over short time scales" and "correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.subcategory: cue-color manipulation confounded by luminance
issues.description: The transient expectation manipulation uses red and blue fixation/cue colors with very different luminance values. Any effect or null effect of cue color is difficult to interpret because perceptual salience and attention differ across colors. This is especially problematic when using cueing and fixation stimuli in a memory task.
issues.quote: both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2).

issues.subcategory: weak manipulation check for transient expectations
issues.description: The claim that participants did not notice the cue-probability contingency rests on an open-ended post-experiment questionnaire. Failure to mention the contingency is not a strong manipulation check and does not establish absence of awareness or presence of learning. The null effect of transient expectations may reflect an ineffective manipulation or inadequate assessment rather than true absence of a mechanism.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: missing exact definition of high-confidence trials
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly analyzes 'high confidence trials' but does not consistently specify which confidence responses counted as high confidence in each experiment, especially given the inconsistent scale reporting in Experiment 1 and the 1-4 scale in later studies. Without this, the analyses are not fully reproducible.
issues.quote: error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response

issues.subcategory: insufficient detail on Bayesian ANOVA priors and settings
issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayes factors from JASP but omits crucial settings such as prior distributions, prior scales, whether default r scales were used, handling of random effects, and whether the reported BFm is against the null or averaged over models. These omissions impede replication and interpretation, especially because model-comparison Bayes factors are sensitive to priors.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.subcategory: appendices/tables referenced but not provided in manuscript body
issues.description: The results repeatedly refer readers to 'Appendix 1 for full model comparison', but the appendix is not included in the provided manuscript text. Since model-selection conclusions depend on those comparisons, the reporting is incomplete.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison

issues.subcategory: use of ANOVA on bounded proportion data with sparse cell counts
issues.description: The dependent variables are relative occurrences/percentages of error types, bounded between 0 and 1 and derived from varying numbers of high-confidence trials. ANOVA on such aggregated proportions can violate normality and homoscedasticity assumptions and ignores binomial precision differences across participants/cells. This is especially problematic given low and variable counts and zero cells. A trial-level generalized mixed model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type... memory delay... and error type... as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: multiple follow-up analyses without adjustment or hierarchy
issues.description: The paper conducts multiple ANOVAs, follow-up ANOVAs split by error type, and follow-up t-tests after selecting best-fitting models. Even in a Bayesian framework, this multiplicity and data-dependent drilling down should be transparently justified and planned. As reported, the inferential pathway is flexible and may overstate evidential strength.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type..." and "BF>1000 in a follow-up t-test

issues.subcategory: misstatement of BF interpretation thresholds
issues.description: The Bayes-factor interpretation thresholds classify BF < 0.33 as 'strong evidence for the null' and 0.33-1 as 'substantial evidence for the null'. This is unconventional and potentially misleading, especially because elsewhere values near 0.45 are called anecdotal evidence against inclusion. The manuscript does not use a consistent interpretive scale.
issues.quote: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis.

issues.subcategory: training/exclusion may induce selection on visual memory ability and confidence
issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants had to pass a separate visual memory training task to enter the study. This procedure selects a subgroup with better change-detection performance and perhaps greater confidence, limiting comparability with later experiments and potentially inflating the apparent prevalence of high-confidence memory effects.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.subcategory: sample limited to psychology students and convenience populations
issues.description: Most samples are young university students, often from first-year psychology courses, and one experiment was collected online on participants' own laptops. The manuscript draws broad conclusions about STM and predictive processing without sufficiently limiting claims to this narrow population and testing environment.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: stimulus domain restricted to overlearned Latin letters
issues.description: The theoretical claims are broad, but the entire paradigm relies on mirrored Roman letters, a highly specialized stimulus class with extreme prior familiarity and strong categorical asymmetry. It is not clear that the findings generalize to visual memory more broadly, to non-letter objects, or to populations with different literacy experiences.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.subcategory: overclaim that findings support predictive processing specifically
issues.description: The discussion presents predictive processing as supported by the data, but the experiments do not test unique predictions of predictive processing against alternative accounts such as familiarity-based response bias, differential discriminability, or retrieval competition. At most, the findings are consistent with several broad reconstructive-memory frameworks.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of fuzzy trace theory
issues.description: The argument against fuzzy trace theory appears conceptually weak. The manuscript claims FTT predicts that high similarity should facilitate false memories and then says abundant false memories with high similarity are inconsistent with the data. But abundant false memories under high similarity is not inconsistent with that prediction. The critique therefore appears internally flawed.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories . This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: response-bias alternative insufficiently ruled out
issues.description: The manuscript dismisses response bias largely because illusion rates increase with delay and differ by target type, but these patterns are still compatible with criterion shifts toward familiar real letters as memory weakens. Experiment 2 equalized probe presence, and Experiment 3 balanced target prevalence, but neither directly estimates decision criteria or signal detection parameters. Thus the conclusion that bias is 'unlikely' is too strong.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias... However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: other-error comparison may be inappropriate baseline
issues.description: The key inference that illusions are special relies on comparing mirrored-counterpart selections to 'other errors.' But the mirrored counterpart is uniquely similar to the target and often category-linked, whereas unrelated distractors are not. Greater frequency of counterpart errors than unrelated errors may reflect ordinary confusion gradients rather than a qualitatively distinct illusion process.
issues.quote: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors

issues.subcategory: online data collection introduces uncontrolled hardware/display variability
issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online on participants' own laptops, yet the task depends on precise visual presentation, timing, and letter mirroring discrimination at 250 ms. The manuscript provides no information about screen size, refresh rate, viewing distance, browser/device restrictions, or timing validation, reducing comparability with in-lab experiments.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment... they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: missing trial counts per analyzed cell after exclusions
issues.description: Because analyses are restricted to high-confidence critical trials and cellwise exclusions were applied, the effective number of observations per participant/cell is crucial. The manuscript reports percentages but not the actual analyzed trial counts by condition after exclusions, preventing assessment of precision and instability.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions

issues.subcategory: extreme exclusion fractions create selection bias across experiments
issues.description: The proportion excluded due to insufficient high-confidence observations varies widely across experiments (e.g., 92/290 in Experiment 2). Such differential attrition makes cross-experiment comparisons difficult and raises concern that the reported consistency is partly due to selecting only high-confidence responders in each dataset.
issues.quote: 92 participants were excluded

issues.subcategory: discrepant delay values across sections
issues.description: The paper alternates between describing short delays as 0.75 s and 0.5 s, and refers in the General Discussion to effects 'from 0.5 s to 3 s' although Experiment 1 used 0.75 s and Experiment 4 used 0.5 s. The summary therefore merges non-identical manipulations, which can mislead readers about the exact temporal evidence.
issues.quote: Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that illusory memories make up a larger part of high confidence responses as time passes (from 0.5 s to 3 s).

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding information
issues.description: There is no reporting of whether experimenters interacting with participants, especially during in-person training, feedback, or Zoom breakout setup, were blind to conditions or hypotheses. Given subjective confidence reporting and extensive experimenter contact in some studies, reporting on blinding would help assess bias risk.
issues.quote: Via the share screen option, participants were given instructions and feedback during the practice block
